name: Colin Gupta

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no tie to employers or AI companies, and what you say stays confidential. How does that sound?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: That's fine; I can be straight with you. I'm 27, single, and came into the utility through a two-year technical diploma. I lead a small line crew, so I'll probably talk about what happens on a wet pole as much as what happens on a screen.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Tell me what a normal working day looks like for you.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I check the overnight faults and the weather before the crew meets at the depot. Then I'm usually setting up a repair, checking the isolation, and climbing or backing up the person who's up there. I like solving a fault with the crew; the part that wears me down is waiting on a road closure or a missing permit while the lights are still out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau: Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the useful bit is getting a cleaner fault list before the crew rolls out. My job is still deciding whether a line is safe to touch, and a shortcut on a screen doesn't make that call for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My pay and hours look steady in that picture, so I don't see a threat to my own income. I already have a good cushion, and I use a few AI tools for quick summaries, but I check anything that affects a crew.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the same storm call rota and the monthly checks on our climbing gear. I'd keep using the fault summary if it saves time, but I wouldn't buy a new system just to say we had one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm, because the hands-on work and the pay both carry on. I still get impatient when software adds another box to tick before we can leave the depot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which part of your day would you most want the software to get right?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The outage location and which crew has the right equipment matter most. A wrong pin can send us to the other side of the valley, and then a family waits longer for power.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you stop trusting one of those summaries?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If it blurred a back-feed risk or left out a damaged pole, I'd stop using it for dispatch. I want the source record beside the summary, because my crew carries the consequence of a bad call.

say: I'd welcome a **cleaner fault list** if it gets my crew to the right outage sooner.
I still need a **lineworker's safety judgment** before anyone touches a live network.
think: My **pay and hours** look steady in this picture.
I use AI summaries, but I check any **crew safety detail** myself.
do: Keep the **storm call rota** and monthly climbing-gear checks.
Use the fault summary only when it saves time and keeps the **source record** visible.
feel: I feel **calm** about my income, though extra software boxes would irritate me.
S0.quote: My job is still deciding whether a line is safe to touch, and a shortcut on a screen doesn't make that call for me.
fieldNote: Colin separates a useful **fault summary** from the safety decision his crew owns.
His strong savings and steady expected pay leave little **personal money pressure** in this scenario.
He would reject software that hides its **source record**.

steps.text: Keep the storm call rota and monthly climbing-gear checks

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption: Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it could take the dull paperwork off a crew lead's plate. I wouldn't tell anyone that line work has vanished; there are still clearances, weather and people waiting below the wires.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our office planning and customer updates could change before my field hours do. I'm not counting on a desk job to be a hiding place, but I can see this affecting my pay less than it affects some of the people booking our work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the company's short course on its new dispatch assistant and test it on a routine outage, with the old map open beside it. I'd keep leading field jobs and ask the scheduler to flag any change in callout hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm calm about my own job for now, but I'd watch the roster closely. Less back-and-forth would be welcome; finding out my crew lost hours after the fact would not be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you check before letting the dispatch assistant guide a crew?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd compare its route and equipment list against the last few jobs on that feeder. If the road access or switching order is wrong once, I want a person to correct the record before it becomes the new default.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who around you would notice the change first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The schedulers would feel it first, especially if routine bookings become one person's screen job. I'd ask Rosa (the crew's senior dispatcher) whether the saved time is turning into more complex work or simply fewer paid shifts.

say: I think **dispatch paperwork** can shrink without ending field repairs.
I'd want the **new route list checked** against the actual feeder and road access.
think: My **field hours** look safer than the office planning work around them.
I don't treat a **desk role** as a guaranteed fallback from AI.
do: Take the **dispatch assistant course** and test it beside the old map.
Keep leading field jobs and check the **callout roster** for lost hours.
feel: I feel **calm about my job**, but I would watch for fewer paid callouts.
S1.quote: I'd ask Rosa (the crew's senior dispatcher) whether the saved time is turning into more complex work or simply fewer paid shifts.
fieldNote: Colin expects planning and customer updates to change before his **field hours** do.
He gives a concrete way to test a route tool against a **known feeder**.
His concern for schedulers is specific but does not yet threaten his own **income**.

steps.text: Take the company dispatch assistant course and test one routine outage
Keep leading field jobs and check the callout roster

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028: Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a system may know every switching rule and still not be the person standing in rain beside a damaged crossarm. The three-year gap before capable field robots matters to my crew, even though it isn't a promise that our jobs last.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect to keep earning through the first year after 2028, because robots for hands-on work are not due until about 2031 in this picture. After that I could lose a big part of my income, and three years is enough to prepare but not enough to know what replaces a whole trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now, I'd raise my monthly savings transfer and ask the lineworkers' association to hold a meeting on the 2031 timetable. In 2029 I'd keep taking field callouts while I compare my bills with a lower-income budget, rather than pretend an office planning role will outlast AGI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm anxious because the work I trained for could lose its physical advantage within the next few years. I have savings and nearby employers, which gives me room to move, but it doesn't tell me what those employers will need after 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your closest friend when you get home that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my friend Dev, who works on another line crew, that our trade has a date on the calendar now. I'd ask him to join the association meeting with me, because a clear answer from the company is better than ten private guesses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which bill would you cut first if the callouts fell before 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd pause big travel and gadget spending first, not the automatic savings transfer or rent. My fixed costs are manageable now, so I'd review actual callout pay every month before changing anything larger.

say: A system may know every **switching rule** and still not stand beside a damaged crossarm.
The **three-year robot gap** matters, but it cannot promise our jobs last.
think: I expect my **income through 2029** to continue before field robots arrive.
I could face **income loss** after 2031 without a clear replacement trade.
do: Raise my **monthly savings transfer** and compare bills with a lower-income budget.
Ask the **lineworkers' association** to meet about the 2031 timetable.
feel: I feel **anxious** about a trade that could lose its physical advantage within a few years.
S2.quote: The three-year gap before capable field robots matters to my crew, even though it isn't a promise that our jobs last.
fieldNote: Colin sees the interval before robots as **preparation time**, not a guarantee.
He anticipates a serious personal income threat after 2031 while naming savings and nearby employers as **sources of control**.
His first cut would be **discretionary purchases**, rather than rent or saving.

steps.text: Raise the monthly savings transfer and cost a lower-income budget
Ask the lineworkers' association to meet on the 2031 timetable

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031: Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew the calendar gives us a chance to plan, not a safe landing. The control room and our planning screens could be different by 2031, while the line work still needs people until robots arrive around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be anxious about income past 2034, but less rushed than in the 2028 picture. I know I can learn new equipment quickly; I don't know whether learning to supervise a robot buys me a lasting career when the robot can eventually do the hands-on job too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd enroll in the utility's high-voltage rescue instructor certificate next year and keep my savings transfer rising. In 2032 I'd use the first year to teach the field procedure while crews still work on the lines, then review whether that income is holding up rather than call it a permanent answer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years lets me make choices with a clear head, but the robot date still sits close behind AGI. I feel uneasy and watchful, not comfortable enough to spend as if nothing is coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What makes that certificate worth the time if physical work changes too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It gives me a real skill to use during the years before the field robots arrive, and the crews need sound rescue practice now. I don't know whether it will pay after 2034, so I won't borrow heavily for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want the company to tell you before 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want a year-by-year plan for field staffing, training costs and callout pay, not a broad promise about new opportunities. If the plan names actual dates and budgets, I can compare it with my own savings and decide whether to stay.

say: Five years gives us **planning time**, not a safe landing.
The **field staffing plan** should name dates, training costs and callout pay.
think: I could be anxious about **income after 2034**, though I have more time than in the fast scenario.
I don't know whether **robot supervision** lasts once robots can do the field work.
do: Enroll in the **high-voltage rescue instructor certificate** next year.
Keep increasing my **savings transfer** and review instructor income in 2032.
feel: I feel **anxious** about work after **2034**, with time to plan but no permanent answer.
S3.quote: I don't know whether learning to supervise a robot buys me a lasting career when the robot can eventually do the hands-on job too.
fieldNote: Colin turns the warning into a **specific certificate**, while openly questioning its long-term value.
He expects income risk after 2034, so the additional lead time does not remove his **job concern**.
He asks for **budgeted staffing information** rather than a promise of new roles.

steps.text: Enroll in the high-voltage rescue instructor certificate next year
Increase the savings transfer and review instructor income in 2032

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036: Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time to make a plan in stages, not enough to ignore the robot date. Our planning tools could change in 2036, and the crews doing repairs would have about three more years before hands-on robots arrive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I have a better chance to build money and try the instructor work before 2039. Still, a thirty-nine-year-old lineworker can't assume the same field income will be there at forty, and I wouldn't call an AI-run office a safe fallback.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep leading crews, add a fixed amount to savings each year, and hold off applying for another field job until the utility publishes real robot trial dates. In 2037 I'd check whether the rescue instructor course still earns work and update my budget; I'd decide about a move only with a real offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm uneasy, but I can see a path through the next few years without betting my whole life on one prediction. The long warning helps me keep choices open, even though the work I love may not be the work I can do forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you change course before 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If my callout hours started falling for two seasons, I'd stop waiting and apply for another utility's field crew lead opening. I'd compare the actual pay and travel first; nearby jobs are plentiful now, but I can't assume that remains true in 2036.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you want to move for work if a good offer came?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd consider moving for a solid offer, but not for a vague promise that a new role might appear. I'm single, so there isn't a partner's job or a child's school tying the decision down, but I'd still want to see the town and the terms before saying yes.

say: Ten years gives me **stages for a plan**, not a reason to ignore the robot date.
I won't treat an **AI-run office** as a safe fallback.
think: I can build **savings and instructor experience** before 2039.
I can't assume my **field income at forty** will match today's.
do: Keep leading crews on the **existing field rota**.
Add a **fixed amount to savings** each year.
Check instructor work in **2037**, and hold off applying elsewhere until robot trial dates are published.
feel: I feel **uneasy**, though a long warning lets me keep several choices open.
S4.quote: The long warning helps me keep choices open, even though the work I love may not be the work I can do forever.
fieldNote: Colin uses the decade for **staged preparation**, not for assuming the trade is permanent.
He would wait for actual **robot trial dates** before making a job move.
His single household makes relocation easier, while he still wants a **real offer** before moving.

steps.text: Keep leading crews on the existing field rota
Add a fixed amount to savings each year

Review rescue instructor work and the budget in 2037

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because it leaves only three years before the field robots arrive. A funded training place, clear dates for robot trials, and a real account of how callout pay changes would help more than a general promise that workers will adapt.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask what happens to the people who still have the skills but aren't needed on the crew. I can save and retrain, but it matters whether the company tells us early enough to use those options.

headlineQuote: I can save and retrain, but it matters whether the company tells us early enough to use those options.
portrait: Colin is a **27-year-old senior lineworker** who leads a small field crew.
His **strong savings** and many nearby jobs give him room to prepare, but not a guaranteed next career.
He welcomes AI for dispatch and summaries while keeping **safety decisions** with the crew.
He feels **watchful about robots** reaching field work, and uses warning time for savings and training.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** leaves only three years before field robots could threaten his trade.
whatWouldHelp: A **funded training place**, clear robot trial dates and honest callout-pay information would help him plan.
